title: The Truth
author: Barrie Wade
summary: Our scriptures teach us to control strong emotions like anger and jealousy. Lines from the Atharva Veda say words can confer strength or drown it, gain friends or turn them into enemies, elevate or lower a person — so we must make our words 'sweet, soft and pleasant'. (The Atharva Veda is one of the four Vedas: Rig, Yajur, Sama and Atharva.)

The poem begins with the old saying 'Sticks and stones may break my bones' but changes its ending: 'But words can also hurt me.' Stones and sticks break only skin, while words are 'ghosts that haunt me' — they keep coming back to the mind.

Harsh words are like swords, 'slant and curved', that pierce and stick inside us. Bats and bricks may cause aches in the bones, but words can 'mortify' (deeply hurt and humiliate) us. The pain from words leaves a scar on the tender mind and heart. Cuts and bruises have healed, 'it's words that I remember'.

Physical injuries heal in time, but the emotional pain caused by unkind words lasts long. We should think before we speak and use kind, polite words, because words can build or destroy relationships. Devices: metaphors (words are ghosts, word swords), contrast between physical and mental pain, alliteration ('sticks and stones', 'bats and bricks'), rhyme (me/me, inside me/mortify me, tender/remember).

sa2: How is the mental pain inflicted on us different from the physical pain?
Physical pain from sticks and stones affects only the skin and bones and heals in time, but mental pain from words haunts us and leaves a lasting scar on the mind and heart.
Why are words referred to as ghosts in the poem 'The Truth'?
Because hurtful words keep coming back to the mind again and again and haunt us long after they are spoken, like ghosts.
What does 'But words can mortify me' mean?
It means that unkind words can hurt and humiliate us deeply.
Why are words compared to swords?
Harsh words pierce and stick inside us like sharp, curved swords, causing deep inner wounds.
What damage does the poet describe in 'The Truth'?
Sticks, stones, bats and bricks break skin and bones, but words haunt, pierce and mortify, leaving scars on the tender mind and heart.
sa3: What is the central idea of the poem 'The Truth'?

Physical injuries from sticks and stones heal, but words can hurt more deeply and for longer; they haunt us like ghosts, pierce like swords and leave scars on the mind and heart. So we should be careful about what we say and use kind, pleasant words.

or: How does the poet change the old saying 'Sticks and stones may break my bones'?

The usual saying ends 'but words will never hurt me'. The poet changes it to 'But words can also hurt me', showing that words hurt even more than physical blows because their pain lasts long after cuts and bruises have healed.
